paras: The killing of Charles Potter was the fatal shooting of Potter, a Black former farm hand also reported as Charles Porter, by the farmer Isaac Chase at Chase's farm in Portsmouth, Rhode Island, near Newport, on February 20, 1903. Chase said he fired in self-defense after Potter had shot at him that morning; he was charged with manslaughter, but a Newport grand jury declined to indict him. Black residents of Newport and Portsmouth raised a fund to bury Potter and investigate, saying they doubted Chase's account.

Potter had once worked for Chase, but the papers disagreed about when he left: one dispatch said he was discharged after a month of altercations, the New-York Tribune said about three years earlier. At the inquest Chase testified that Potter had left in August three or four years before and had not been seen since. Little was known of him locally until a letter from Isaac Porter of Woodstown, New Jersey, suggested the dead man was his son.

According to accounts that came largely from Chase, Potter appeared on the morning of February 20 as Chase and his 16-year-old daughter set out in a sleigh. The Providence News said Potter accused Chase of "undue familiarity with a woman" and fired a revolver at him and his daughter, missing, then ran off. Chase telephoned Sheriff Anthony of Newport, who sent him to the town sergeant or constable; no officer came. Meanwhile a party of farmers, called a "posse" by the Tribune and the wire, hunted Potter for several hours before giving up.

Chase armed himself and patrolled in front of his house. About 2 o'clock Potter returned, and by Chase's account he advanced toward the house with his hand in his pocket, whereupon Chase fired one shot and killed him. Early reports named a shotgun, but the Sun learned the next day that it was a rifle. A loaded revolver and a razor were found on the body. Chase telephoned the sheriff and offered to surrender, and deputy sheriffs took him to the county jail in Newport.

On February 21 Chase was arraigned for manslaughter, pleaded not guilty and was released on $10,000 bail. The lawyer Frank F. Nolan said Potter had complained to him days earlier that Chase had defamed his character. Black residents raised a fund for burial and an investigation, and a Newport dispatch said their action led Chase to ask the sheriff for protection. Accounts of the burial differ: the Providence News reported a funeral from Mount Zion church on February 26, while a later dispatch said the father took the body to Salem County, New Jersey.

Coroner George E. Hicks held a three-hour inquest at the Portsmouth town hall on February 26, with Nolan representing the dead man's friends. Chase testified that Porter had accused him of disgracing his name, which he denied, and other witnesses agreed on the facts; no inquest verdict appears in the coverage. The district court hearing was postponed while the inquest continued, and on April 14 the grand jury returned no true bill against Chase.

All the coverage found came from white newspapers, and the wire carried the story as far as Georgia, Kansas and Wisconsin. Headlines put Potter's alleged attempt first: the Savannah Morning News ran "NEGRO RAISED ROW ON VANDERBILT'S FARM," and the Daily Kennebec Journal "IN SELF-DEFENSE" over "Farmer Obliged to Kill an Ugly Negro." The Portland Daily Press printed that dispatch as "A BAD NEGRO"; it said Chase "was obliged to take the law into his own hands."

The New York Sun noted "a strong feeling against the colored farmhands on the island" and reported a general opinion that Chase would be acquitted. The Providence News, the fullest local source, gave Chase's version and suggested Potter was "demented," but also reported the Black residents' doubts and the inquest. Later wire items carried the Black residents' protest and Nolan's statement, the latter under the subhead "Victim Had Complained of Defamation of His Character."

The account of the shooting came from Chase, and the first wire report said there was no witness to it. Black residents doubted his self-defense claim, and Potter's lawyer described a grievance that Chase denied at the inquest.

reader.title: Killing of Charles Potter
bases: A single farmer, Isaac Chase, shot his former farm hand Potter at his own farm after an earlier pursuit by a party of farmers had failed; no posse or group was present at the killing (A2, A4, A5, A8).

Potter was killed by one man, Chase, who claimed self-defense, was charged with manslaughter and was not indicted (A2, A8, A22); the earlier farmers' pursuit did not catch him (A2, A4), so no group of three or more did the killing.

The local Providence News, a New-York Tribune special, the New York Sun and the wire all report that Chase shot Potter at his Portsmouth farm on February 20 (A1, A2, A4, A6); Black residents disputed only his self-defense account (A11, A12).

accounts.label: Chase's account
accounts.gist: Potter quarreled with him and fired a revolver at him in the morning; returning in the afternoon, he advanced toward the house with his hand in his pocket, and Chase, fearing another attempt on his life, shot him.

accounts.label: Inquest witnesses
accounts.gist: Witnesses at the coroner's inquest were reported to agree substantially as to the morning's events as published.

accounts.label: Black residents of Newport and Portsmouth
accounts.gist: Doubted the accuracy of Chase's tale and were not satisfied he acted in self-defense; raised a fund to investigate.

accounts.label: Potter's lawyer
accounts.gist: Nolan said Potter had told him days before that Chase had defamed his character and that he would act for himself if the lawyer did nothing; Chase denied any grievance.

framing.detail: Wire headlines 'NEGRO RAISED ROW ON VANDERBILT'S FARM' and 'TRIES TO KILL A FARMER' put Potter's alleged attempt first.
'IN SELF-DEFENSE. Portsmouth, R. I., Farmer Obliged to Kill an Ugly Negro'; says Chase 'was obliged to take the law into his own hands'.
The Sun reported the arrest on a murder charge, noted strong feeling against colored farmhands, and predicted acquittal.
The Providence News gave Chase's account and townsmen's self-defense view, called Potter possibly 'demented', but later reported Black residents' doubts and the inquest.
'FARMER KILLS A NEGRO. Victim Had Complained of Defamation of His Character' carried the victim's side via his lawyer.

conflicts.note: The Sun on February 22 corrected its shotgun report to a rifle; Chase spoke of his rifle at the inquest (A15), so the rifle is the better-supported version.
